Very good game in the vein of Orwell and Hypnospace Outlaw. It's also very lean, nothing ends up feeling extraneous to the story being told. - atmosphere

NEUTRAL:
- game time - on one hand the price is fair for it, but on the other hand the game feels like it's missing bits after about half point mark - which means it would benefit if it was a bit longer
- writing is all over the place ranging from great/clever to cheesy in a bad way (characters especially)

CONS:
- about last third of the game; denouement is abrubt and feels like devs wanted to execute too many points too fast which culminates with general feel of rush writing and ending that just doesn't live up to what ingame Day 1 and 2 have set; investigation results felt like a letdown
- no replay value

The Operator has a lot of good things going for it, the premise and story are interesting and the puzzle gameplay keeps itself fresh so nothing feels tedious. Special mention must be made about the high quality of the sound design - both the voice acting and the choice and timing of the music stings are excellent.

The biggest problem with The Operator for me is that it all falls apart just as it was gaining momentum. The last set of puzzles lack the sense of discovery from earlier, the game abruptly ends leaving a bunch of unanswered questions, and you're left feeling like nothing you did mattered.

This feels like the kind of game that should have multiple endings or changes caused by the player decisions, but there is nothing like that here. This is a specific story that you're being taken on a ride for - one with a pretty obvious "twist" - and no replayability.

If this was a prologue or chapter one of a larger game I would feel more favourable to this, but in its current state I wouldn't recommend this unless it's at least half price.

If you want to feel like you're an investigator for the US government in an agency like the FBI or CIA, this game puts you there. It's more than a visual novel, but less than a full-fledged world with practically infinite choices.

Even so, it feels full and like the choices matter. Definitely some memorable moments in this. I would like a full-fledged game with many choices and outcomes, but that would deserve a higher price tag. This is what it should be for the price, and isn't too short.

The story is solid and engaging. Having worked in the government, I can say this is idealized a bit, but is definitely not ridiculous compared to crime shows. I was surprised at several points in the plot, and the way you discover the protagonist's situation and that he encounters is solid.

However, there are a few things that make it a bit realistic. It is set in the early 90s, yet the "FDI" (not FBI) have the capability to "enhance" photos like Stable Diffusion can now. There are cell phone towers and tracking, but not many people used cell phones in the US back at that time, and the ones that did had big Motorolla boxes the size of a lunch box they plugged into. They were technically mobile, but not very. The cell phone antenna had to be attached to the car roof with a magnet. And it cost over $100/mth. Sure, it wasn't uncommon for business people, and really rich people had somewhat smaller mobile phones, but still.

Also, in the boot screen, it shows a version of Linux that is "x86_64", but 64 bit didn't become really common until around 2007.

However, you can forgive these small foibles since you can consider the game as a parallel universe world; very similar, but slightly different, like how you work for the FDI instead of FBI. Perhaps in this world, they had a decade or two jump on us in technology.

I thoroughly enjoyed this and hope they put out a longer game with either more choice or perhaps getting to play more characters, or a single protagonist through a longer story arc. When it comes down to it, my only complaint with this game is that there wasn't more of it. That's a good complaint to have if it matches up with a good price, and it does. Good luck to the dev team now and in the future!

Additionally, in terms of puzzles, they are all fairly straight forward and don't really make much use of the tools the game introduces. Aside from the tool you use to look up people, most of the programs and documents introduced in the game are used a single time.

Like everything, there’s the good, the bad and the ugly.

The good is that it’s quite a good experience, even if the puzzles are simple and intuitive, they’re not repetitive, and there’s some variety to it. The plot is extremely well written and serves well the thematics of the game.

The bad is that I feel like somethings were underdeveloped. I’m referring specifically to the puzzles, I think like at least the chemical compound/molecules breaking could have appeared a couple more times. Not only that, I think the puzzles could experience a little bit more of variety, like 1-2 more types of puzzles. Although the plot was great, it also could have dived a bit further.

The ugly is how the story breaks on the climax to an open ending. The story was just building up throughout the first two hours. During the 3rd hour, it was building the suspense to the climax, and then it’s just ends abruptly. The game could be double its playtime and still have room for a sequel, if the developers/publishers wanted to sell more content later on, during the next couple months (through a DLC) or down the road. However, the story is unfinished. It does leave mixed feelings like many are referring down on the comments and on their reviews.

The game is incomplete as it is. The endgame was too soon and didn’t develop where it should.

Nonetheless, this is common in movies and books, and I see where the developer can come from, as it may take a lot of time to put a game, even with this size, on the market and well polished.

I will do this: I’ll leave a positive review on this game, but if there is a sequel, which I expect it will have, and if the game isn’t finished by then, cuts again abruptly and is the same length, I will leave a negative review on the next one.
